newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Schengen will not create police state-presidency.
newsitem.headline: Schengen will not create police state-presidency.

text.p: The presidency of the European Union's Schengen agreement on Thursday rejected claims by Greek protesters that the open-border pact would create a police state.

The protesters outside the Greek parliament, which on Wednesday adopted Schengen, said the pact would turn Europe into a giant police state with citizens' personal data available to authorities through a computer network.

"The idea of a police state is completely without foundation. The exchange of information between states will be about suspected criminals, not about all their citizens," said Regina Lima of the office of Portugal's Under-Secretary for European Affairs.
The office manages the six-month rotating presidency of Schengen, held by Portugal until the end of June.
"People can circulate freely under Schengen. This is an advantage, not a disadvantage," Lima told Reuters. "The agreement does not harm people's freedom."
The 300-seat Greek parliament voted 142-80 -- 78 deputies were absent - for the Schengen agreement, which already has seven full members including France and Germany.

Schengen, which provides for border controls between EU member states to be removed and for increased cooperation on police matters, was backed by the ruling Greek socialist party and the main opposition conservatives.
However, 53 conservative deputies ignored their party line and voted against, while outside the parliament building some 1,000 demonstrators held a rally.

Lima, who welcomed the Greek parliament's adoption of Schengen, rejected charges by some protesters who said that identity cards to be issued to EU citizens under the pact would carry the number 666 in their bar code, the sign of Satan.
"There are no plans to issue identity cards to citizens in the Schengen area, much less to stamp them with the number 666," she said.
A number of countries, including Greece, have passed laws governing limits on the type of information the state can hold on citizens, but debate continues on whether Schengen threatens privacy.

France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Spain, Portugal and Germany are all full Schengen members. Greece, Austria, Italy, Denmark, Finland and Sweden have signed but not yet fully implemented the pact.
